FURLOUGH (TEMPORARY REDUCTION IN WORK OR PAY) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS FURLOUGH INFORMATION SHEET
This Furlough (Temporary Reduction in Work or Pay) — Information Sheet is prepared with respect to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., in the position of Software Engineer, beginning a period of reduced or suspended work on March 16, 2026. As used in this document, "furlough" refers to an employer-initiated, ordinarily temporary, interruption of an employee's usual work and pay — a full or partial reduction in scheduled hours, or a full suspension of work for a defined or expected period — where the employer does not treat the employment relationship itself as ended and generally anticipates the employee's return. This document addresses a question the rest of this project's Ending Employment documents generally assume has already been answered — that a termination, layoff, or discharge has definitely occurred — by instead examining the narrower, specifically-defined thresholds at which a temporary reduction in work or pay starts to trigger some of the same statutory notice duties, benefit-continuation rights, and wage-and-hour consequences that apply to a full separation, even though the employer does not consider the employee separated. It describes: how California's WARN Act (Cal/WARN) and the federal WARN Act each define the kind of event that triggers their own notice duties, and how a furlough relates to each definition; how California's unemployment insurance law treats a week of reduced hours or reduced pay; how the federal salary-basis regulation for exempt employees treats a deduction from salary tied to a furlough; and how federal COBRA regulations treat a reduction in hours as a possible qualifying event for continued group health coverage. This document deliberately does not restate this corpus's existing California WARN Act, federal WARN Act, exempt employee's final-week salary, COBRA, Cal-COBRA, or unemployment insurance claimant information sheets — each of which addresses its own statute in more general depth — and instead focuses narrowly on how a temporary, employer-initiated furlough interacts with the specific triggering definitions each of those statutes and regulations uses. This document does not determine that any specific reduction in Jordan Lee's hours or pay at Acme, Inc. is, or is not, a furlough, a layoff, or a termination for any particular legal purpose, and it does not calculate any specific notice deadline, benefit amount, or continuation-coverage election deadline.

"FURLOUGH" IS NOT ITSELF A DEFINED LEGAL TERM IN ANY SOURCE THIS DOCUMENT ADDRESSES
None of the statutes or regulations described in this document use the word "furlough" as a defined term of its own. California's Cal/WARN statute defines "layoff"; the federal WARN Act defines "employment loss"; California's unemployment insurance law defines when an individual is "unemployed"; the federal salary-basis regulation for exempt employees describes when a salary deduction is or is not permitted; and the federal COBRA regulations define "reduction of hours" and describe when that reduction causes a "loss of coverage." Each of these sources uses its own defined vocabulary, tied to its own statutory purpose, and this document maps the commonly used word "furlough" to each source's own terms separately rather than assuming that qualifying as one (for example, a "reduction of hours" under the COBRA regulations) automatically means qualifying as another (for example, a "layoff" under Cal/WARN, which by its own text requires a "separation from a position").

CAL/WARN'S OWN DEFINITION OF "LAYOFF" REQUIRES A SEPARATION FROM A POSITION
California's WARN Act (Cal/WARN) does not use the word "furlough" anywhere in its own definitions section. It instead defines "layoff" — one of the three kinds of events (along with "relocation" and "termination") that can trigger the statute's notice duty for a covered establishment — to mean "a separation from a position for lack of funds or lack of work." On the statute's own text, this definition is built around a "separation from a position," a phrase Cal/WARN's definitions section does not itself further define. A reduction in an employee's hours or a period of unpaid time off, standing alone, is not obviously the same thing as a "separation from a position" in the way that phrase is ordinarily understood, and Cal/WARN's own text does not resolve whether, or at what point, a furlough becomes a "separation" for purposes of this definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Layoff” means a separation from a position for lack of funds or lack of work."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code § 1400.5, subdivision (c), definition of "layoff" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1400.5(c)), used as real evidence of how Cal/WARN itself defines the event that (together with a covered-establishment size threshold and other conditions this clause does not restate) can trigger its notice duty — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer's or employee's situation, and not a determination that any specific reduction in hours or pay is or is not a "layoff" within this statute's meaning. This corpus's existing California WARN Act (Cal/WARN) — Information Sheet independently cites and quotes several other subdivisions of this same statutory section, § 1400.5 — subdivisions (a), (b), (d), (e), (f), (g), and (h) — for the covered-establishment, employer, mass-layoff, relocation, termination, and employee definitions; this clause cites subdivision (c), the "layoff" definition, which that existing document does not quote. This clause does not resolve the undefined term "separation from a position" itself, and does not determine how long a furlough must last, or how definite or indefinite its expected end date must be, before it would be treated as such a separation. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific reduction in the employee's hours or pay at the employer does or does not meet this definition.

FEDERAL WARN ACT'S "EMPLOYMENT LOSS" DEFINITION SEPARATELY REACHES AN EXTENDED REDUCTION IN HOURS
The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act defines the trigger for its own notice duty differently from Cal/WARN's "layoff" definition. Federal law defines "employment loss" to mean any of three things: an employment termination other than a discharge for cause, voluntary departure, or retirement; a layoff exceeding six months; or a reduction in hours of work of more than 50 percent during each month of any six-month period. This third category does not require that the employee's position be eliminated or that the employee be separated at all — an employee who keeps their job title and keeps working, but whose hours are cut by more than half in every month across a six-month span, has experienced an "employment loss" under this federal definition, a result that does not obviously follow from Cal/WARN's own, narrower "layoff" definition (a "separation from a position") described in a companion clause of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "subject to subsection (b), the term “employment loss” means (A) an employment termination, other than a discharge for cause, voluntary departure, or retirement, (B) a layoff exceeding 6 months, or (C) a reduction in hours of work of more than 50 percent during each month of any 6-month period;"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2101(a)(6) (Cornell LII text), 29 U.S.C. § 2101(a)(6), definition of "employment loss" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2101)
  Known gap: This is federal law (29 U.S.C. § 2101(a)(6)), applicable nationwide, used as real evidence of how the federal WARN Act itself defines the event that can trigger its notice duty — not a claim about whether any specific employer or specific reduction in the employee's hours meets the federal Act's separate size, duration, and covered-employer thresholds for "plant closing" or "mass layoff," which this clause does not restate. This corpus's existing federal WARN Act document independently cites and quotes this same statutory section's plant-closing and mass-layoff definitions (§ 2101(a)(2) and (a)(3)) and its 90-day aggregation rule (§ 2102(d)); this clause cites the same section's "employment loss" definition itself, § 2101(a)(6), which those existing citations do not quote. This clause's own reference to "subject to subsection (b)" points to a further statutory carve-out (for certain temporary facilities and strikes or lockouts, among other things) that this clause does not independently describe. This session attempted a CourtListener case-law search relevant to how courts have applied the reduction-in-hours prong of this "employment loss" definition to a furlough or similar temporary reduction; the search returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (CourtListener's 125-request/day quota, already exhausted from other research this session), so no case law is cited in this document, and this clause proceeds on the statutory text alone rather than on any recollection of case law. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical both times, with no normalization needed. This document is informational only and does not itself determine that any specific reduction in the employee's hours meets this definition.

A WEEK OF REDUCED HOURS CAN ITSELF MAKE AN EMPLOYEE "UNEMPLOYED" FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE PURPOSES
California's Unemployment Insurance Code does not require a complete separation from employment before an individual can be treated as "unemployed" for a given week. The statute separately defines an individual as "unemployed" for any week of less-than-full-time work if the wages payable to the individual for that week, reduced by $25 or by 25 percent of those wages (whichever amount is greater), do not equal or exceed the individual's weekly benefit amount. This is a distinct basis for "unemployed" status from the more familiar case of a week in which the individual performs no work and no wages are payable at all; it is the basis that can apply to an employee who is furloughed for part of a week, or whose hours are cut but not eliminated, rather than an employee who is not working at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any week of less than full-time work, if the wages payable to him or her with respect to the week, when reduced by twenty-five dollars ($25) or 25 percent of the wages payable, whichever is greater, do not equal or exceed his or her weekly benefit amount."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(2), reduced-hours "unemployed" test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1252.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(2)), used as real evidence of California's own reduced-hours eligibility test — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claimant's situation, and not a determination that the employee or any other specific claimant qualifies as "unemployed" for any specific week, meets the separate eligibility conditions the Unemployment Insurance Code imposes elsewhere, or would actually receive any particular benefit amount. This corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet and Severance Pay and Unemployment Insurance Eligibility Information Sheet each independently cite and quote different subdivisions of this same statutory section — § 1252(a)(1) (no work performed, no wages payable) and § 1252(c) (definition of "wages" for this section) — for a different point, about whether severance or dismissal pay counts as "wages payable" for a week; this clause cites § 1252(a)(2), the reduced-hours/reduced-wages test itself, which those existing citations do not quote, and does not restate their severance-pay analysis. This clause does not describe the statute's own weekly-benefit-amount calculation, work-search requirements, or any other eligibility condition found elsewhere in the same chapter. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical after normalizing the same expected per-request debug-timestamp and ViewState-token noise described in a companion clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself file a claim, calculate a benefit amount, or determine eligibility for any specific week.

A DEDUCTION TIED TO LACK OF AVAILABLE WORK CAN ITSELF DEFEAT EXEMPT SALARY-BASIS STATUS
The federal regulation defining what it means to pay an employee on a "salary basis" — a requirement for most federal overtime-exemption categories — states that an employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions from the employee's predetermined compensation are made for absences that the employer, rather than the employee, occasions, or that the operating requirements of the business occasion. The same provision states directly that if the employee is ready, willing, and able to work, deductions may not be made for time when work is simply not available. This is a different rule from the general full-week rule addressed elsewhere in this project's Exempt Employee's Pay in the Final (and First) Week of Employment document, which concerns a week in which the employment relationship itself begins or ends partway through; this rule instead concerns a week of continuing employment in which the employer furloughs an otherwise-exempt employee for part of the week because work is not available, and states that deducting pay for that kind of partial-week, employer-caused absence can itself cost the employee their exempt salary-basis status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions from the employee's predetermined compensation are made for absences occasioned by the employer or by the operating requirements of the business. If the employee is ready, willing and able to work, deductions may not be made for time when work is not available."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2), deductions for employer-occasioned absences (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  Known gap: This is federal law (29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2)), applicable nationwide regardless of which state's law otherwise governs the employment relationship. This corpus's existing Exempt Employee's Pay in the Final (and First) Week of Employment document independently cites and quotes § 541.602(a) (the general salary-basis rule) and, by its own description, the full-week exception within § 541.602(a)(1); this clause cites the immediately following subdivision, § 541.602(a)(2), which addresses a legally distinct scenario — a mid-employment furlough rather than a week bookended by hiring or termination — and does not restate that existing document's first/last-week analysis. This clause does not address the regulation's separate list of specific, narrow exceptions in § 541.602(b) (for example, full-day disciplinary suspensions or full-day personal absences), which can permit a deduction in other circumstances this clause does not describe; whether any of those specific exceptions applies to a particular furlough is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause also does not determine whether the employee's position is properly classified as exempt in the first place, which is a separate, threshold question this document does not address. This document is informational only.

FEDERAL COBRA REGULATIONS TREAT A TEMPORARY LAYOFF AS A KIND OF "REDUCTION OF HOURS"
The Treasury Department's own regulations implementing COBRA describe, in detail, what counts as a "reduction of hours" of a covered employee's employment — one of the events that can be a COBRA "qualifying event." The regulation states that a reduction of hours occurs whenever there is a decrease in the hours the covered employee is required to work or actually works, but only where the decrease is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment, and that this is true regardless of whether the employee keeps performing services after the reduction. The regulation's own examples name a temporary layoff specifically: an absence from work due to disability, a temporary layoff, or any other reason (other than an FMLA leave) counts as a reduction of hours under this definition if it is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A reduction of hours of a covered employee's employment occurs whenever there is a decrease in the hours that a covered employee is required to work or actually works, but only if the decrease is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(e) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(e), definition of "reduction of hours" (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-54/section-54.4980B-4)
  Known gap: This is federal law (26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(e), a Treasury regulation), applicable nationwide. This corpus's existing COBRA Election Notice document independently cites and quotes the statutory list of COBRA qualifying events at 29 U.S.C. § 1163, including "termination ... or reduction of hours" as one category; this clause instead cites the Treasury Department's own implementing regulation, a different source (a regulation rather than the underlying statute), for its more granular definition of what "reduction of hours" itself means — a definition the statute's own text does not spell out, and which the existing COBRA document's citation to § 1163 does not quote. This clause's example naming "a temporary layoff" is the regulation's own illustrative example, not this document's characterization; the regulation does not use the word "furlough." Naming this event as a "reduction of hours" is a separate question from whether it actually causes a "loss of coverage" sufficient to make it a COBRA qualifying event — a further condition addressed in the next clause of this document, which this clause does not resolve. The regulatory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from ecfr.gov, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical after normalizing the same per-request CSP-nonce noise described in a companion clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific reduction in the employee's hours at the employer is a COBRA qualifying event.

A REDUCTION OF HOURS IS A COBRA QUALIFYING EVENT ONLY IF IT ACTUALLY CAUSES A LOSS OF COVERAGE UNDER THE PLAN'S OWN TERMS
Naming an event as a "reduction of hours" is not, by itself, enough to make it a COBRA qualifying event. The same Treasury regulation states that an event only satisfies this part of the qualifying-event test if, under the terms of the particular group health plan, the event causes the covered employee (or the employee's spouse or dependent child) to lose coverage under that plan — and defines "lose coverage," for this purpose, to mean ceasing to be covered under the same terms and conditions that applied immediately before the event. A furlough or other reduction of hours that does not actually change the employee's coverage under the specific group health plan's own eligibility terms — for example, because the plan's own rules keep a furloughed employee enrolled for some defined period regardless of hours worked — does not meet this loss-of-coverage condition and, on this regulation's own terms, is not a COBRA qualifying event merely because hours were reduced.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An event satisfies this paragraph (c) if, under the terms of the group health plan, the event causes the covered employee, or the spouse or a dependent child of the covered employee, to lose coverage under the plan. For this purpose, to lose coverage means to cease to be covered under the same terms and conditions as in effect immediately before the qualifying event."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(c) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(c), definition of "lose coverage" (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-54/section-54.4980B-4)
  Known gap: This is the same federal regulation (26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4) as the preceding clause, but a different subdivision — Q&A-1(c), the loss-of-coverage condition, rather than Q&A-1(e), the reduction-of-hours definition — so the two clauses are not independent sources of each other, though together they state the regulation's two-part test. This clause does not describe how any particular group health plan's own eligibility terms treat a furloughed employee, which is a plan-specific fact this document does not resolve, and does not describe the regulation's separate bankruptcy-specific loss-of-coverage rule (also part of the same Q&A-1(c)) or its statement that a loss of coverage need not occur immediately after the event, so long as it occurs before the end of the maximum coverage period — points this clause does not quote or further address. The regulatory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from ecfr.gov, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical after normalizing the same per-request CSP-nonce noise described in a companion clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether the employer's own group health plan treats the employee's furlough as causing a loss of coverage, and does not determine that any COBRA notice obligation has or has not been triggered.

NOTICE OF FURLOUGH
Acme, Inc. provides this notice to Jordan Lee, in the position of Software Engineer, regarding a furlough — a temporary reduction or suspension of work — described as follows.

Furlough start date: March 16, 2026
Expected return-to-work date, if known: April 13, 2026, or "Not yet determined"
Weekly salary or wage rate before this furlough: $1,800 per week
Reduced hours per week during this furlough, if the furlough is partial rather than a full suspension of work (enter 0 if work is fully suspended): 0

During this furlough, Acme, Inc. states the following regarding continuation of group health plan coverage, if any: _______________________________________________

Acme, Inc. does not, by this notice, treat Jordan Lee's employment relationship as ended, and Acme, Inc. states that its present expectation is that Jordan Lee will return to work as described above. This notice does not itself determine Jordan Lee's eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits, continuation health coverage, or any other benefit during the furlough period, and does not waive, modify, or expand any right or obligation either party otherwise has.

RETURN-TO-WORK / END-OF-FURLOUGH ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This acknowledgment confirms that the furlough described in the Notice of Furlough dated March 16, 2026, between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee, has ended.

Actual return-to-work date: _______________________________________________
If this date differs from the expected return date originally stated (April 13, 2026, or "Not yet determined"), the reason stated by Acme, Inc. is: _______________________________________________
Hours and pay rate upon return: _______________________________________________

Both Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee acknowledge that this document records the end of this specific furlough period and does not itself resolve any dispute about wages, benefits, or notice that may have arisen during the furlough.

Employee signature: _______________________ Date: _____________
Employer representative signature: _______________________ Date: _____________

THIS DOCUMENT STATES FACTS ABOUT THE LAW; IT DOES NOT DETERMINE WHETHER ANY SPECIFIC FURLOUGH COMPLIES WITH IT
This Furlough Information Sheet describes selected statutory and regulatory definitions and rules that can bear on a temporary reduction in Jordan Lee's work or pay at Acme, Inc. — from Cal/WARN, the federal WARN Act, California's unemployment insurance law, the federal salary-basis regulation for exempt employees, and the federal COBRA regulations. It does not describe every law that could apply to a furlough, including state and local paid-sick-leave, disability, or predictive-scheduling laws that this document's research did not address. It does not calculate any notice deadline, benefit amount, or continuation-coverage election deadline, and it does not determine that Acme, Inc.'s furlough of Jordan Lee, as actually carried out, does or does not comply with any of the sources described above.

The statute separately defines an individual as "unemployed" for any week of less-than-full-time work if the wages payable to the individual for that week, reduced by $25 or by 25 percent of those wages (whichever amount is greater), do not equal or exceed the individual's weekly benefit amount. This is a distinct basis for "unemployed" status from the more familiar case of a week in which the individual performs no work and no wages are payable at all; it is the basis that can apply to an employee who is furloughed for part of a week, or whose hours are cut but not eliminated, rather than an employee who is not working at all.

This clause does not describe the statute's own weekly-benefit-amount calculation, work-search requirements, or any other eligibility condition found elsewhere in the same chapter. expectedJSON.body: The federal regulation defining what it means to pay an employee on a "salary basis" — a requirement for most federal overtime-exemption categories — states that an employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions from the employee's predetermined compensation are made for absences that the employer, rather than the employee, occasions, or that the operating requirements of the business occasion. The same provision states directly that if the employee is ready, willing, and able to work, deductions may not be made for time when work is simply not available. This is a different rule from the general full-week rule addressed elsewhere in this project's Exempt Employee's Pay in the Final (and First) Week of Employment document, which concerns a week in which the employment relationship itself begins or ends partway through; this rule instead concerns a week of continuing employment in which the employer furloughs an otherwise-exempt employee for part of the week because work is not available, and states that deducting pay for that kind of partial-week, employer-caused absence can itself cost the employee their exempt salary-basis status.

citations.quote: An employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions from the employee's predetermined compensation are made for absences occasioned by the employer or by the operating requirements of the business. If the employee is ready, willing and able to work, deductions may not be made for time when work is not available.

This clause does not address the regulation's separate list of specific, narrow exceptions in § 541.602(b) (for example, full-day disciplinary suspensions or full-day personal absences), which can permit a deduction in other circumstances this clause does not describe; whether any of those specific exceptions applies to a particular furlough is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause also does not determine whether the employee's position is properly classified as exempt in the first place, which is a separate, threshold question this document does not address. expectedJSON.body: The Treasury Department's own regulations implementing COBRA describe, in detail, what counts as a "reduction of hours" of a covered employee's employment — one of the events that can be a COBRA "qualifying event." The regulation states that a reduction of hours occurs whenever there is a decrease in the hours the covered employee is required to work or actually works, but only where the decrease is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment, and that this is true regardless of whether the employee keeps performing services after the reduction. The regulation's own examples name a temporary layoff specifically: an absence from work due to disability, a temporary layoff, or any other reason (other than an FMLA leave) counts as a reduction of hours under this definition if it is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment.

citations.quote: A reduction of hours of a covered employee's employment occurs whenever there is a decrease in the hours that a covered employee is required to work or actually works, but only if the decrease is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment.

expectedJSON.gap: This is federal law (26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(e), a Treasury regulation), applicable nationwide. This corpus's existing COBRA Election Notice document independently cites and quotes the statutory list of COBRA qualifying events at 29 U.S.C. § 1163, including "termination ... or reduction of hours" as one category; this clause instead cites the Treasury Department's own implementing regulation, a different source (a regulation rather than the underlying statute), for its more granular definition of what "reduction of hours" itself means — a definition the statute's own text does not spell out, and which the existing COBRA document's citation to § 1163 does not quote. This clause's example naming "a temporary layoff" is the regulation's own illustrative example, not this document's characterization; the regulation does not use the word "furlough." Naming this event as a "reduction of hours" is a separate question from whether it actually causes a "loss of coverage" sufficient to make it a COBRA qualifying event — a further condition addressed in the next clause of this document, which this clause does not resolve. expectedJSON.body: Naming an event as a "reduction of hours" is not, by itself, enough to make it a COBRA qualifying event. The same Treasury regulation states that an event only satisfies this part of the qualifying-event test if, under the terms of the particular group health plan, the event causes the covered employee (or the employee's spouse or dependent child) to lose coverage under that plan — and defines "lose coverage," for this purpose, to mean ceasing to be covered under the same terms and conditions that applied immediately before the event. A furlough or other reduction of hours that does not actually change the employee's coverage under the specific group health plan's own eligibility terms — for example, because the plan's own rules keep a furloughed employee enrolled for some defined period regardless of hours worked — does not meet this loss-of-coverage condition and, on this regulation's own terms, is not a COBRA qualifying event merely because hours were reduced.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(c) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.quote: An event satisfies this paragraph (c) if, under the terms of the group health plan, the event causes the covered employee, or the spouse or a dependent child of the covered employee, to lose coverage under the plan. For this purpose, to lose coverage means to cease to be covered under the same terms and conditions as in effect immediately before the qualifying event.

expectedJSON.gap: This is the same federal regulation (26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4) as the preceding clause, but a different subdivision — Q&A-1(c), the loss-of-coverage condition, rather than Q&A-1(e), the reduction-of-hours definition — so the two clauses are not independent sources of each other, though together they state the regulation's two-part test. This clause does not describe how any particular group health plan's own eligibility terms treat a furloughed employee, which is a plan-specific fact this document does not resolve, and does not describe the regulation's separate bankruptcy-specific loss-of-coverage rule (also part of the same Q&A-1(c)) or its statement that a loss of coverage need not occur immediately after the event, so long as it occurs before the end of the maximum coverage period — points this clause does not quote or further address.
